title: Prospective evaluation of confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) for intraoperative in vivo differentiation of tumor progression and radiation necrosis in cerebral metastases.
summary:
Background: After radiation therapy for brain metastases, it is often very difficult to distinguish on an MRI scan whether an abnormal area in the brain is recurrent tumor growth or just scar tissue caused by the radiation (so-called radiation necrosis). However, making this distinction is crucial for the surgical treatment strategy.   

Study Objective: This study investigates whether digital in-vivo microscopy (ZEISS Convivo) can close this gap by evaluating the tissue directly in real time. The goal is to establish optical criteria that allow surgeons to reliably distinguish living tumor tissue from pure radiation necrosis during the operation.   

Procedure: During the regularly scheduled surgery, patients are given a dye (sodium fluorescein) to make the tissue more visible. The surgeon then briefly places a sterile miniature probe of the laser microscope against the diseased tissue to take digital microscopic images. In addition, extracted tissue samples are briefly scanned right in the operating room before being sent to the pathology department for standard microscopic examination.
conditions: Secondary malignant neoplasm of brain and cerebral meninges

interventions.name: Intraoperatively (during tumor resection): Following the administration of sodium fluorescein (standard of care), the sterile confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) probe is applied to defined tissue areas (tumor center and margin) to acquire digital in-vivo microscopic images. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age > 18 years.   
History of radiotherapy or radiosurgery for a brain metastasis.   
Radiological progression with an indication for surgery or biopsy.   
Written informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
Known allergy to fluorescein.   
Renal insufficiency (GFR < 30 ml/min) or severe liver dysfunction (Child-Pugh B/C).   Pregnancy or breastfeeding.   
Inability to provide informed consent.
